text: I remember the violet light of the courtyard, the smells of a warm spring evening. The mothers were making dinner, it was time to go home, but we delayed, challenging each other, without ever saying a word, testing our courage. For some time, in school and outside of it, that was what we had been doing. Lila would thrust her hand and then her whole arm into the black mouth of a manhole, and I, in turn, immediately did the same, my heart pounding, hoping that the cockroaches wouldn’t run over my skin, that the rats wouldn’t bite me.

source.name: Diane Rehm Show, Readers' Review: My Brilliant Friend (Scribd excerpt embedded on the page)

passages.attribution: Excerpt from My Brilliant Friend by Elena Ferrante. Translation by Ann Goldstein. Copyright © 2012 by Edizioni E/O. First publication 2012 by Europa Editions. Used with permission.

notes.author: Elena Ferrante is the pseudonym of an Italian novelist who has never appeared in public. My Brilliant Friend is the first of the four Neapolitan novels, translated by Ann Goldstein.
notes.work: The narrator, Elena, now in her sixties, recalls her childhood friendship with Lila in a poor neighbourhood of Naples in the 1950s. This passage comes from the first page.

observed.narrativeVoice: retrospective first person; the adult narrator recalls herself as a child
observed.proseStyle: plain, concrete diction in long cumulative sentences joined by commas
observed.rhythm: long sentences that accumulate clauses; a repeated pattern of Lila acting and the narrator copying
observed.pacing: moves from one remembered evening back to a habit of many days
observed.imagery: the violet light of the courtyard, the black mouth of a manhole, cockroaches and rats

techniques.name: Mirroring
techniques.text: each dare Lila performs is followed by the narrator doing the same, which sets up their relationship in the structure of the sentences.

techniques.name: Retrospective frame
techniques.text: "I remember" places a distant adult voice over the child's fear.

techniques.name: Unspoken contest
techniques.text: the girls challenge each other "without ever saying a word", so the rivalry is shown only through what they do.

interpretation.tone: tense and intimate; fear held at a remembered distance

locator.end: that the rats wouldn't bite me.
locator.where: Childhood, The Story of Don Achille, chapter 1, first page

text: Felled, dazed, silent, he has fallen; knocked full length on the cobbles of the yard. His head turns sideways; his eyes are turned toward the gate, as if someone might arrive to help him out. One blow, properly placed, could kill him now.

Blood from the gash on his head—which was his father’s first effort—is trickling across his face. Add to this, his left eye is blinded; but if he squints sideways, with his right eye he can see that the stitching of his father’s boot is unraveling.

source.name: Macmillan, Wolf Hall book page (Read Excerpt)

passages.attribution: Excerpt from Wolf Hall by Hilary Mantel. Copyright © 2009 by Hilary Mantel. Published by Henry Holt and Company.

notes.author: Hilary Mantel (1952–2022) was an English novelist. Wolf Hall and its sequel Bring Up the Bodies both won the Booker Prize.
notes.work: The first novel of a trilogy about Thomas Cromwell at the court of Henry VIII. It opens in 1500 with the young Cromwell beaten by his father, Walter.

observed.narrativeVoice: close third person, held to the boy's senses; he is not yet named
observed.proseStyle: short clauses and semicolons; exact physical detail; plain modern English
observed.rhythm: staccato opening ("Felled, dazed, silent"), then longer sentences of observation
observed.pacing: slowed to seconds; one moment on the cobbles is examined in detail
observed.imagery: blood across the face, the cobbles of the yard, the unravelling stitching of the father's boot seen with one eye

techniques.name: In medias res
techniques.text: the chapter opens on a shouted command and a body already on the ground.

techniques.name: Withheld identity
techniques.text: the boy is only "he"; the reader is placed inside him before knowing who he is.

techniques.name: Close detail
techniques.text: the injured eye notices the stitching of the boot coming loose, a small exact detail amid the violence.

interpretation.tone: brutal and unflinching, observed without self-pity

locator.where: Part One, I, Across the Narrow Sea, Putney, 1500, opening

text: In the second half of the 1960s I traveled repeatedly from England to Belgium, partly for study purposes, partly for other reasons which were never entirely clear to me, staying sometimes for just one or two days, sometimes for several weeks. On one of these Belgian excursions which, as it seemed to me, always took me further and further abroad, I came on a glorious early summer's day to the city of Antwerp, known to me previously only by name.

source.name: Penguin Random House Canada, Austerlitz excerpt

passages.attribution: Excerpt from Austerlitz by W. G. Sebald, translated by Anthea Bell. Published by Penguin Random House.

notes.author: W. G. Sebald (1944–2001) was a German writer who lived in England; his books mix fiction, travel, memoir and photographs. Austerlitz was his last novel.
notes.work: An unnamed narrator recounts his meetings, over decades, with Jacques Austerlitz, who slowly recovers his lost childhood. This is the novel's opening, in Antwerp.

observed.narrativeVoice: retrospective first person; an unnamed narrator recalling his own uncertain movements
observed.proseStyle: long, formal sentences with many subordinate clauses; measured, slightly old-fashioned diction
observed.rhythm: extended periodic sentences that defer their main point
observed.pacing: unhurried and digressive; travel described as drift
observed.imagery: few images; a glorious early summer's day and a city "known to me previously only by name"

techniques.name: Admitted uncertainty
techniques.text: the narrator travels "for other reasons which were never entirely clear to me", so his account begins in doubt.

techniques.name: Cumulative sentence
techniques.text: clauses pile up within each sentence and defer its point, so the journey reads as drift.

techniques.name: Hedged perception
techniques.text: "as it seemed to me" qualifies even the direction of his travels.

locator.start: In the second half of the 1960s
locator.end: known to me previously only by name.

text: My name is Kathy H. I'm thirty-one years old, and I've been a carer now for over eleven years. That sounds long enough, I know, but actually they want me to go on for another eight months, until the end of this year. That'll make it almost exactly twelve years. Now I know my being a carer so long isn't necessarily because they think I'm fantastic at what I do. There are some really good carers who've been told to stop after just two or three years. And I can think of one carer at least who went on for all of fourteen years despite being a complete waste of space.

source.name: KCRW, Excerpt from Never Let Me Go

passages.attribution: Excerpt from Never Let Me Go by Kazuo Ishiguro. Copyright © 2005 by Kazuo Ishiguro. Published by Alfred A. Knopf. Excerpt supplied by Dial-A-Book.

notes.author: Kazuo Ishiguro, born in Nagasaki in 1954 and raised in England, received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2017.
notes.work: Kathy H. looks back on her years at Hailsham, an English boarding school, and on her friends Ruth and Tommy. This is the novel's opening.

observed.narrativeVoice: first person, conversational, addressed to a listener
observed.tense: present for her situation, past for her record
observed.proseStyle: plain, colloquial diction ("a complete waste of space"); short sentences
observed.rhythm: short declarative sentences with frequent self-corrections
observed.pacing: a calm self-introduction that gives facts without explaining them
observed.imagery: few images; the passage works through institutional terms rather than pictures

techniques.name: Unexplained terminology
techniques.text: "carer", and being "told to stop" after a set number of years, are stated as ordinary facts, so the reader must infer the world.

techniques.name: Self-correction
techniques.text: Kathy qualifies her own claims ("That sounds long enough, I know, but actually"), building an anxious, modest voice.

techniques.name: Direct address
techniques.text: she speaks as if to someone who already knows her world.

text: I told you last night that I might be gone sometime, and you said, Where, and I said, To be with the Good Lord, and you said, Why, and I said, Because I’m old, and you said, I don’t think you’re old. And you put your hand in my hand and you said, You aren’t very old, as if that settled it. I told you you might have a very different life from mine, and from the life you’ve had with me, and that would be a wonderful thing, there are many ways to live a good life. And you said, Mama already told me that. And then you said, Don’t laugh! because you thought I was laughing at you.

source.name: Macmillan, Gilead (Oprah's Book Club) book page (Read Excerpt)

notes.author: Marilynne Robinson, born in 1943, is an American novelist and essayist. Gilead won the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2005.
notes.work: John Ames, an elderly pastor in Gilead, Iowa, writes a long letter to his young son, to be read when the boy is grown. This is its opening.

observed.narrativeVoice: first person, epistolary; a father writing to his young son
observed.tense: past for last night's conversation, inside a present-tense letter
observed.proseStyle: plain words in one long sentence of reported speech without quotation marks
observed.rhythm: a chain of "and you said … and I said" clauses that move like conversation
observed.pacing: slow; one small exchange is given in full
observed.imagery: the child's hand in the old man's hand

techniques.name: Epistolary address
techniques.text: the narrator speaks to "you", a son who will read the letter only as a grown man.

techniques.name: Polysyndeton
techniques.text: repeated "and" joins the turns of the conversation into one unbroken sentence.

techniques.name: Unmarked dialogue
techniques.text: speech is reported without quotation marks, so voices sit inside the writer's memory.

interpretation.tone: tender and reflective, aware of death without fear

locator.start: I told you last night that I might be gone sometime
locator.end: because you thought I was laughing at you.
